sounds.intro: Hieroglyphs write consonants only, so we know which consonants a word had far better than how it sounded. Scholars reconstruct the sounds from Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian written with vowels, from Greek and cuneiform spellings of Egyptian names, and from related Afroasiatic languages. The values below are reconstructions, and several are disputed; the 'like' column also gives the classroom convention for reading aloud.

rows.like: said 'a' in class; probably a glottal stop, the catch in 'uh-oh'
rows.note: Older loanwords suggest an r- or l-like sound that later weakened.

rows.like: said 'i' in class; a 'y' sound, or a glottal stop at the start of a word
said 'a' in class; really a throaty sound like Arabic ʿayn
rows.note: In some words it seems to come from an older d.

rows.like: 'w' as in 'wet', or 'u' where a vowel is needed
a tapped r; there was no separate letter for l, which was written with r or n
rows.note: A final r often dropped in speech: nfr 'good' became Coptic ⲛⲟⲩϥⲉ noufe.

rows.like: a strong breathy h from the throat, like Arabic ḥāʾ
said 's'; once a different sound, perhaps z
rows.note: Merged with 𓋴 by the Middle Kingdom. Some books transliterate it z.

rows.like: a k made further back in the throat
'd' in class; probably an emphatic t
rows.note: Coptic writes it as t: dj 'give' became ϯ ti.
Coptic writes it ϫ: ḏd 'say' became ϫⲱ djō.

tips.p: Hieroglyphs write only consonants, so the vowels of Egyptian are lost. Egyptologists slip an e between consonants to make words sayable: nfr 'nefer', ḥtp 'hetep', sḏm 'sedjem'. This is a convention for reading aloud, not a reconstruction.

By convention ꜣ and ꜥ are both read 'a', j is read 'i' and w 'u' where a vowel is needed: ꜥnḫ 'ankh', jmn 'imen', ḥtp dj nswt 'hetep di nesu'. ṯ is said like the ch of 'church' and ḏ like the j of 'judge'.

Coptic, written in Greek letters from the 3rd century AD, shows real vowels: nṯr 'god' became ⲛⲟⲩⲧⲉ noute, rmṯ 'people' ⲣⲱⲙⲉ rōme, ꜥnḫ 'life' ⲱⲛϩ ōnh and kmt 'Egypt' ⲕⲏⲙⲉ kēme. Sounds shifted over two thousand years, so these are clues rather than Middle Egyptian itself.

Foreigners wrote Egyptian names with vowels. Greek writers give Amenōphis for Jmn-ḥtp (Amenhotep) and Thoutmōsis for Ḏḥwtj-ms (Thutmose). Cuneiform letters from Amarna call Amenhotep III Nimmureya, from his throne name Nb-mꜣꜥt-rꜥ, and Akhenaten Napḫururiya, from Nfr-ḫprw-rꜥ, so nfr began with something like 'nap' in the 14th century BC.
The consonants are fairly secure. The exact values of ꜣ, ꜥ, d, ḏ, g and q are debated, and stress and vowels can only be guessed from much later evidence.

grammar.title: Masculine and feminine
grammar.note: Feminine words end in -t, the bread loaf 𓏏. The determinatives 𓀀 and 𓁐 show a man or a woman and are not read.

grammar.note: Two nouns side by side mean 'of'. A suffix on a noun means 'my, your, his'.

grammar.title: Adjectives
grammar.note: An adjective follows its noun and agrees with it in gender and number.

grammar.title: Suffix pronouns
grammar.note: On a noun they mean 'my, your, his'; after jw or a verb they are the subject. =j is often written with the speaker's determinative, 𓀀 or 𓁐, or not at all.

grammar.note: These stand at the head of 'who' sentences: jnk sꜣ=k 'I am your son'.

grammar.title: The offering formula
grammar.note: The prayer on Middle Kingdom stelae, false doors and coffins. Its parts are taught across units 6, 9 and 10.
head: Part
Egyptian
Meaning
rows: an offering that the king gives
so that he may give an invocation offering
for the ka of the honoured N

grammar.title: The past: sḏm.n=f
grammar.note: Verb + .n + subject. Verbs ending in j drop it in writing, so jrj 'do' gives jr.n=f.
head: Subject
sḏm 'hear'
jrj 'do'
Meaning
rows: the king heard, the king did

grammar.title: Prepositions
grammar.note: Prepositions take nouns or suffixes: n=j 'to me', ḥnꜥ=f 'with him'.
head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: jw=f m pr 'he is in the house'
jw nswt ḥr st=f 'the king is on his throne'
jj.n=s r pr 'she came to the house'

grammar.title: Dependent pronouns
grammar.note: Used as the object of a verb and as the subject after an adjective or nn. They come straight after the word they lean on.
head: Person
Pronoun
Example
rows: ḥzj ṯw nswt 'may the king praise you'

grammar.title: The stative (pseudoparticiple)
grammar.note: Describes a state, or a finished movement with verbs like jj 'come'. Endings follow Allen's Middle Egyptian; the 3rd person masculine .w is usually not written.

grammar.title: Numbers
grammar.note: Numbers are tallies: repeat a sign to add it up, so 𓎆𓎆𓎆 is 30. They follow the noun, which usually stays singular.

grammar.title: Singular, dual and plural
grammar.note: Plurals are written with three strokes 𓏥 or a sign drawn three times, as in 𓊹𓊹𓊹 nṯrw 'gods'. The dual is for pairs: tꜣwj 'the Two Lands'.

grammar.title: Infinitives
grammar.note: The infinitive follows r in the future construction. Verbs ending in j, and šmj, add t.
head: Verb

Example
rows: jw=n r mꜣꜣ nswt 'we will see the king'

prt m hrw 'going out by day'
jw=f r šmt r ẖnw 'he will go to the Residence'

grammar.title: Negation
grammar.note: n negates verbs, nn denies that something exists or is there, m forbids. n sḏm=f is past, n sḏm.n=f is present or 'cannot'.
head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: he did not hear my voice
there is no one in the house
he is not in the house

grammar.title: Questions
grammar.note: jn makes a yes-or-no question; question words often take pw 'it'.
head: Word
Use
Example
rows: jn ntk sꜣ=j 'are you my son?'

grammar.note: Commands, participles and the indirect genitive are everywhere in teachings, tales and spells.
